title: SMITH v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
In the case of Smith v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Smith, is a British citizen who identifies as a Gypsy by birth, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Her case highlights the acute vulnerability faced by Gypsy families in the United Kingdom, particularly regarding access to lawful and stable accommodation that respects their cultural traditions. For decades, Ms. Smith and her family led a nomadic life in Surrey, moving frequently due to the lack of available official or private sites for Gypsies. Despite repeated applications for authorised sites and attempts to secure stable housing, they were consistently turned away due to full waiting lists and restrictive local policies. In 1993, Ms. Smith purchased a plot of land in Runnymede and moved her family’s caravan there, only to be denied planning permission on the grounds that the land was in a protected Green Belt area. Her appeals were dismissed, and she faced enforcement action, leaving her family at risk of eviction and further instability.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), among others. The case was declared admissible, but no violation was ultimately found. Smith v. the United Kingdom is significant as it underscores the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller families face in securing lawful accommodation, reflecting broader patterns of exclusion and the tension between planning laws and minority rights in late 20th-century Britain.
